name: Freya Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a crew leader at Highmoor Electric, a small co-op owned by the farms and villages it serves up in the hills. Mornings I plan the day with my crew of three, then we drive out to whatever's broken: a pole a tractor clipped, a line sagging after ice, or a new connection for a barn. I also fly the co-op's inspection drone, because I was the only one who wanted to learn it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that people know us. Mrs Okafor at the dairy brings us coffee when we're on her road. What wears me out is money: co-op pay is lower than at the big utility down the valley, I'm still paying off my diploma, and I help my little brother with his college fees, so there's never more than a few weeks in the bank.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. I'll read you five short pictures of the future and ask a few questions about each.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Go for it. I use AI tools every day, for study, checking my sums and reading manuals, so I've got opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. I use these tools every day and they help, but if that's as far as it goes, fine. I'd post a picture of my crew in the mud with something like: the robots aren't coming, back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I'm stuck where I am: good at the job, underpaid, and three weeks from broke. I'd hoped the new tech would open a door, like a drone program I could run. Without it, the co-op stays small and so does my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep using AI to study for my advanced line certificate, which gets me a pay grade. I'd offer drone photos of roofs and fields to farmers on weekends, maybe sixty a job. And I'd set up an automatic transfer of a hundred a month into savings the day after payday, before I can spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little flat. Like a storm forecast that never shows up: you're relieved, but you'd already charged all the batteries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which is it, disappointed or relieved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, honestly. Relieved for the older men on my crew, disappointed for me. I'm twenty-seven and I wanted a bigger change than a better spell-checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would pay sixty for drone photos?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farmers checking storm damage on barn roofs, mostly. Jonas at the sheep farm asked me last spring, and I did it for a box of eggs. If I charged everyone like Jonas, I'd have a lot of eggs.

say: I'm a bit **disappointed**, because AI helps me every day but stops there.
I'd post a picture of my crew **in the mud**: the robots aren't coming.
think: I'm **stuck**: good at the job, underpaid and three weeks from broke.
Without new tech, the **co-op** stays small and so does my pay.
do: Use AI to study for the **advanced line certificate** and its pay grade.
Sell **drone photos** of barn roofs to farmers on weekends.
Set up an **automatic transfer** of a hundred a month after payday.
feel: **Flat**, relieved for older crew members but disappointed for myself.
S0.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I wanted a bigger change than a better spell-checker.
fieldNote: She's the rare person **disappointed** that AI stays small, because she wanted a door to open.
Her money squeeze comes from a **diploma loan** and her brother's college fees.
She already has a **side-income** idea built on the co-op's drone skills.

steps.text: Study for the advanced line certificate with AI help
Charge farmers sixty a job for drone roof photos
Set up an automatic hundred-a-month savings transfer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for crews if co-ops like ours get a say. The office side, billing, call answering and planning routes, will change a lot, and I'd say out loud that we should keep those people and retrain them. Online I'd write a long post about it that nobody reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's my chance. Someone has to run the sensors, read the drone data and teach the crews, and I'm already the one doing it for free. If the co-op turns that into a proper role, I get a pay grade and I still climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a one-page plan for the board in the first month: sensors on the worst ten miles of line, the drone flying every week, and me running it. I'd do the advanced drone licence the co-op keeps putting off. And I'd show Ben and Kwame on my crew how to use the inspection app, so nobody gets left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly excited. This is the first picture where my job gets better instead of just harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the board says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take the plan to the big utility down the valley, they'd probably say yes, and the co-op would lose me. I don't want that, because I believe in co-ops. But I've got a brother in college and three weeks of savings, so I can't wait forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the office staff. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carla on billing and the two women who answer the phones in storms. They know every member by voice. I'd want them trained to run the outage map, not shown the door, and I'd say so at the members' meeting.

say: This is good news for crews if **co-ops** like ours get a say.
We should keep and **retrain** the billing and phone staff, not let them go.
think: It's my **chance**, because I already run the drone and sensors for free.
A proper role means a **pay grade**, and I still get to climb.
do: Give the board a **one-page plan** for sensors and weekly drone flights in month one.
Take the **advanced drone licence** the co-op keeps putting off.
Teach my crew the **inspection app** so nobody gets left behind.
feel: **Calm** and mostly **excited**, because my job gets better instead of harder.
S1.quote: Someone has to run the sensors, read the drone data and teach the crews, and I'm already the one doing it for free.
fieldNote: She's the only one in her crew who sees a **promotion** in the change, not a threat.
Loyalty to the **co-op** clashes with a thin cushion that won't let her wait.
She speaks up for the **billing and phone** staff by name.

steps.text: Hand the board a one-page plan for line sensors and drone flights
Teach two crew members the inspection app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment co-ops were made for. If the members own the robots, the savings come back as lower bills instead of going to shareholders. I'd say it at every members' meeting until they put it in the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's scary even for me. By 2028 the planning and the drone analysis, the stuff I was proud of learning, a machine does better. Then by 2031 the climbing goes too, and I'm thirty-two with a loan and no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a robotics technician course this winter, the online one with weekend practicals in the city, and pay for it by selling my old motorbike. I'd ask the co-op to make me the person who trains and maintains whatever robots they buy. If they won't, I'd apply to the robot makers' field teams, even if it means moving to the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with my hands busy. Fear is easier when you've got a plan for Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between 2028 and 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my runway. For three years the thinking parts are gone but the hands-on work is still mine, so I'd climb by day and study by night. By the time robots arrive, I want to be the one who fixes them when they fall off a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving to the city cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hills, my crew and Mrs Okafor's coffee, which sounds small but isn't. City rent would eat any pay rise. I'd do it, but I'd hate it.

say: This is the moment **co-ops** were made for.
If members own the **robots**, the savings come back as lower bills.
think: By 2028 a machine does the **drone analysis** I was proud of learning.
By 2031 the climbing goes, and I'm thirty-two with a **loan** and no savings.
do: Start an online **robotics technician** course this winter, paid for by selling my motorbike.
Ask the co-op to make me its **robot trainer** and maintainer.
Apply to robot makers' **field teams** if the co-op says no, even in the city.
feel: **Anxious**, but easier with my hands busy and a plan for Tuesday.
S2.quote: By the time robots arrive, I want to be the one who fixes them when they fall off a pole.
fieldNote: She treats the **three-year gap** as a runway: climb by day, study by night.

steps.text: Enrol in an online robotics technician course this winter
Sell the motorbike to pay the course fees
Ask the co-op for the robot maintenance role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do it properly and too short to waste a year arguing. I'd push the co-op to start a training fund now, with the members' approval. And I'd say it on the regional union forum too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, five years feels about right for me. I could finish a proper robotics diploma part-time, still climb, and be ready when the robots come in 2034. The money's still thin, but time is the thing I was short of in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a two-year part-time robotics diploma next autumn, with the co-op paying half if I sign to stay three years. I'd keep the drone side business going to cover the other half. And I'd help write the co-op's robot plan, so the members vote on it instead of a supplier deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense. Like the night before a big job you've prepared for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sign to stay three years. Doesn't that trap you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The co-op gave me my first job when the big utility wouldn't look at a girl with a diploma from the hills. Three years for a diploma is a fair trade, and I'd rather owe the co-op than a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother to pick a course where he uses his hands and his head, like I'm trying to do. He's studying accounting, which worries me more than my own job. I'd say it kindly, over dinner, not as a lecture.

say: Five years is enough to do it **properly**, but too short to waste arguing.
The co-op should start a **training fund** now, with members' approval.
think: Five years feels **about right** to finish a robotics diploma and still climb.
Money is still thin, but **time** is what I lacked in the fast picture.
do: Start a **part-time robotics diploma** next autumn, half paid by the co-op.
Keep the **drone side business** going to cover the other half.
Help write the co-op's **robot plan** so members vote on it.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way, like the night before a job you've prepared for.
S3.quote: The co-op gave me my first job when the big utility wouldn't look at a girl with a diploma from the hills.
fieldNote: Her worry shifts from herself to her **brother**, who is studying accounting.
She'd sign a **three-year stay** for training out of loyalty to the co-op.

steps.text: Start a part-time robotics diploma next autumn
Keep selling drone roof photos to farmers
Draft the co-op's robot plan for a members' vote

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody should be thrown away in this one. Ten years is enough to retrain a whole workforce. I'd push hard for the government to fund it, and I'd say so loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be thirty-nine when the robots come, with ten years of learning behind me. My worry would be the older men on the crew and the office staff, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the advanced line certificate first, then the robotics diploma, no rush. I'd save properly for the first time, two hundred a month once the diploma loan is paid off in 2028. And I'd stand in the co-op's board elections, because whoever's on the board in 2035 decides what happens to the crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even. The future looks like a job I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. What could go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. Ten years is long enough to talk yourself into waiting. I've seen good lineworkers sit on their hands because the change was always five years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because decisions about robots will be made in a room, and right now nobody in that room has climbed a pole. A co-op lets members vote, so a lineworker can actually get in. I'd want to be in that room in 2035.

say: Nobody should be **thrown away** when there's ten years to retrain.
The **government** should fund retraining for the whole workforce.
think: I'd be **fine**, thirty-nine with ten years of learning behind me.
My worry is the **older crew** and the office staff, not me.
do: Finish the **advanced line certificate**, then the robotics diploma.
Save **two hundred a month** once the diploma loan is paid off in 2028.
Stand in the co-op's **board elections** before 2035.
feel: **Calm**, even excited, because the future looks like a job I'd want.
S4.quote: Decisions about robots will be made in a room, and right now nobody in that room has climbed a pole.
fieldNote: Her only fear for herself is **getting comfortable** and waiting too long.
She wants a lineworker on the co-op **board** when robot decisions are made.
With time, her money plan finally includes **real saving**.

steps.text: Finish the advanced line certificate, then the robotics diploma
Save two hundred a month once the loan is cleared

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even the skills I learned to stay ahead get taken first, and I'd have no money to retrain. What would help is paid study time, a few hours a week the employer has to give you, plus help with course fees for people on lower pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my brother's generation. I'm worried about kids choosing courses right now, like accounting, for jobs that won't be there. Someone should tell them honestly, before they take on the debt.

headlineQuote: I'm worried about kids choosing courses right now, like accounting, for jobs that won't be there.
portrait: Freya Garcia, 27, leads a **three-person crew** at a small hill-country electricity co-op.
She uses **AI tools daily** and flies the co-op's inspection drone.
A **diploma loan** and her brother's fees keep her savings under a month.
She sees **Steady Disruption** as a promotion and stays calm with ten years' warning.
Her answers keep returning to **co-op ownership** and members deciding about robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her newest skills go first and she has no money to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid study time** from employers, plus help with course fees for lower-paid workers.
